470.title: Dhul-Qarnayn's wall
470.hook: a just king builds a barrier of iron and copper for a people and calls it a mercy (18:83–98)
470.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Dhul-Qarnayn as a model of just rule: power used to protect the weak, without payment, and credited to God; scholars have long debated his identity without agreement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boat, the boy and the wall. Your line was there was a reason. Today, our last day in al-Kahf.

The last story in al-Kahf starts with a question people put to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: tell us about Dhul-Qarnayn. The name means the one with two horns, or the man of two ages, or of two ends of the earth; the commentators offer several. He's a ruler given power and the means to use it. He travels to where the sun sets, then to where it rises, and then to a pass between two mountains, where a frightened people wait for him.

The people at the pass, the surah says, could hardly understand speech. But they manage to say it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj, Gog and Magog, are ruining the land. Will you build a barrier between us and them if we pay you? Dhul-Qarnayn turns the money down. What my Lord has given me is better, he says. Help me with your strength instead. Bring me blocks of iron. They stack the iron until it fills the gap between the mountainsides. Then: blow, and they work the bellows until the iron glows like fire. Then: bring me molten copper to pour over it. The wall holds; the raiders could neither climb it nor dig through it. Now the line this day is built on. Standing before what he built, he says, in Pickthall's words: "This is a mercy from my Lord". And: when my Lord's promise comes, He will level it to the ground, and my Lord's promise is true. Earlier in this surah, a man walked through his gardens saying this will never perish. Here a man stands before iron and copper and says: it's a mercy, and it will fall when God decides. Who was Dhul-Qarnayn? Muslim scholars have long disagreed: some said Alexander the Great, some Cyrus of Persia, some an ancient king of Yemen. The Qur'an doesn't say. It tells what he did with power: he refused payment, put people to work on their own protection, and gave the credit away. In the modern four-trials reading, that completes the set: faith in the cave, wealth in the garden, knowledge by the sea, and power at the wall.

Picture one small barrier you could help build with them, not for them: a bedtime, a budget, a boundary, a lock that works. And picture handing the credit away when it holds.
Dhul-Qarnayn's wall. Iron and molten copper across a mountain pass, built with the people's own hands, and called a mercy from God. Today's word.
Your line: a mercy from my lord. Built with strength, credited to God. Day four hundred seventy.

471.title: A call in secret
471.hook: Zakariyya's bones are weak and hair white, but he's never been disappointed in prayer (19:3–4)
471.howItsDone: Many Muslims make private du'a, often at night, for long-held wishes such as children, and cite Zakariyya's prayer in 19:3–6 and 21:89 as a model of quiet persistence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhul-Qarnayn's wall. Your line was a mercy from my Lord. Today, a new surah.

Surah nineteen is named for a woman: Maryam, the mother of 'Isa, the only woman the Qur'an names. But it doesn't open with her. It opens with an old man, alone, at night, praying so quietly that nobody else could hear. He's been asking for the same thing for years. Today: his prayer, and the sentence in it that has kept people asking ever since.

The old man is Zakariyya, Zechariah, a guardian of the temple and of the young Maryam. In Pickthall's words, the surah calls this a mention of God's mercy to His servant, "When he cried unto his Lord a cry in secret". Nida'an khafiyya: a hidden call. Why hidden? Commentators suggest humility, or the late hour, or that he was embarrassed to ask, at his age, for a child. Then he describes himself honestly: my bones have grown weak, and my head is ablaze with white hair. And then, in Pickthall's words: "and I have never been unblest in prayer to Thee, my Lord." Look at the logic. He doesn't say: I've always gotten what I asked for. He says: I've never come away from asking You empty. His case for asking again isn't his strength, which is gone, or his wife's, who has never had a child. It's his history with God. Asking has always been good for him, so he asks. He asks for an heir, to carry on the family of Ya'qub. The answer comes: a son, named Yahya, a name, the surah says, given to no one before him. When Zakariyya asks for a sign, he's told he won't speak to people for three nights, though nothing is wrong with him. A man who prayed in secret is given silence. A hadith in Muslim's collection sits beside this: a person's prayer is answered as long as they don't grow impatient and say, I prayed and prayed and saw nothing, and give up.

If you don't, just hold the wish and notice whether you'd given up on it, and whether you want to.

472.title: Yahya, gentle
472.hook: Yahya is given wisdom as a child and is dutiful and gentle to his parents (19:12–15)
472.howItsDone: Muslims honor Yahya as a prophet and son of Zakariyya; his portrait in 19:12–15 is often taught to young people as a model of wisdom joined with gentleness toward parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nida'an khafiyya, Zakariyya's hidden call. Your line was never disappointed in asking.

A child an old couple waited years for. You might expect him to be spoiled: every wish granted, every tantrum forgiven, the center of a house that had been quiet a long time. The Qur'an gives us that child, the son of Zakariyya, the answer to the secret call. In four short verses it describes who he grew up to be, and it's almost the opposite of spoiled. Today: Yahya.

Christians know him as John the Baptist. In the Qur'an he's Yahya, and Surah Maryam gives him a short portrait. Verse twelve: he's told to hold fast to the scripture, and given hukm, wisdom, judgment, while still a child. Verse thirteen: and hanan from Us, and purity, and he was mindful of God. Hanan is tenderness, the softness of compassion, described as coming from God's own presence. Then verse fourteen, in Pickthall's words: "And dutiful toward his parents. And he was not arrogant, rebellious." Barr, dutiful, shares a root with birr al-walidayn, the name Muslims give to the goodness to parents that Al-Isra commands. And the two things he wasn't: jabbar, overbearing, someone who forces his will on others, and 'asiyy, disobedient. A boy given wisdom early could easily have grown proud of it, the kid who knows better than his old parents. Instead the portrait puts wisdom and tenderness side by side, and the gentleness lands on the people closest to him, the father and mother who'd waited so long. Then verse fifteen marks the three great thresholds of a life: "Peace on him the day he was born, and the day he dieth and the day he shall be raised alive!" Born, dying, raised. A few verses later in this same surah, 'Isa, his cousin in the tradition, says nearly the same words about himself. Two prophets, each wrapped in peace from beginning to end.

If they've died, let this be a memory you hold gently.

473.title: "O my father"
473.hook: Ibrahim pleads with his father gently four times, and parts with, peace be upon you (19:41–47)
473.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite Ibrahim's words in 19:42–47 as the model for speaking to parents who don't share one's faith: gently, respectfully, and without abandoning conviction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yahya, wise as a child and tender to his parents. Your line was gentle, not proud.

Politics at the holiday table. A career. A marriage. Faith. An argument with a parent about something that matters can start calm and end with someone leaving the room. Surah Maryam has one of these conversations, between a young man and his father, and the subject is God. It starts calm and ends badly. But the way the son leaves the room is the whole lesson. Listen for how he begins each sentence.

The son is Ibrahim. His father, named Azar in another surah, makes and serves idols. Ibrahim begins each of his four sentences the same way: ya abati. O my father. Grammarians note that this form of address is tender, something like my dear father. One: my father, why worship what can't hear, can't see, and can't help you at all? Two: my father, knowledge has come to me that hasn't come to you, so follow me, and I'll guide you on a level road. Three: my father, don't serve Shaytan. Four: my father, I'm afraid a punishment from the Merciful will touch you. The fourth isn't a threat. It's fear for him. Then the father answers: do you turn away from my gods, Ibrahim? If you don't stop, I'll stone you. Get away from me for a long time. Plenty of arguments end right there. Ibrahim's reply, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Peace be unto thee!" Salamun 'alayk. Then: I'll ask my Lord to forgive you; He has always been kind to me. And: I'll withdraw from you and from what you call on, and I'll call on my Lord. He leaves without slamming the door, and without giving up his conviction. Both are true at once. The Qur'an is honest that the story goes further: At-Tawbah says that later, when it became clear his father was set against God, Ibrahim dissociated himself from him. But in this moment, threatened with stoning, he answers with peace, and a promise to pray.

474.title: Love appointed
474.hook: the Merciful will appoint love for those who believe and do good (19:96)
474.howItsDone: Muslims cite 19:96 and the hadith of Jibril's call when speaking of the love people feel for the righteous; teachers emphasize doing good sincerely, for God, rather than to be admired.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ya abati, Ibrahim's four gentle pleas. Your line was peace be upon you, father. Today, our last day in Surah Maryam.

Some people are like this: not the loudest at the party, not the most famous, not the one working hardest to be liked. And yet when their name comes up, faces soften. Neighbors bring them soup when they're sick. Their funeral, when it comes, is full. Nobody can quite say how it happened. Near the end of Surah Maryam, a verse names what happened, and who did it.

Verse ninety-six, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! those who believe and do good works, the Beneficent will appoint for them love." The Beneficent is ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, a name of God that comes back again and again in Surah Maryam. The word for love is wudd: warm, steady affection, the kind that lasts. It shares its root with one of God's names, al-Wadud, the Loving. And the verb is sa-yaj'alu: He will make, He will place, He will appoint. Love here isn't earned like a wage or chased like a prize. It's placed, by God, in hearts. Whose hearts? Some commentators said other people's, so the good are loved by those around them. Some said: between the believers themselves. Some said: God's own love for them. The Arabic leaves room for all three. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim draws the picture. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: when God loves a servant, He calls Jibril and says, I love this person, so love them. And Jibril loves them. Then Jibril calls out to the people of heaven: God loves this person, so love them. And the people of heaven love them. Then acceptance is placed for them on earth. It starts in heaven and arrives on earth last; the neighbor bringing soup is the end of a long chain. And the verse asks people to believe and do good. It doesn't say: try to be liked. Surah Maryam opened with Zakariyya calling in secret, then Yahya's tenderness and Ibrahim's peace. It closes with love that is given, not grabbed.

475.title: Not to distress you
475.hook: We did not send the Qur'an to make you miserable (20:2)
475.carry: the stones were never the point
475.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 20:2, 2:185 and the hadith 'the religion is ease' to warn against making religion a burden; Taha is also used as a given name, from the opening letters of this surah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: love appointed. Your line was love will be appointed. Today, a new surah.

Some people carry their faith like a backpack full of stones. Every missed prayer is a stone. Every slip is a stone. They're trying so hard that the thing meant to hold them up is wearing them down. If that's ever been you, or someone you love, Surah twenty has something to say first. It opens with two Arabic letters, and then, in its very first sentence, tells the Prophet what the Qur'an is not for.

The two letters are Ta and Ha. Like the other letters that open some surahs, their meaning is debated. Some read Ta-Ha as a name for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and Taha is given as a boy's name for that reason. Others said it means O man, in an old dialect. Others simply said: God knows best. Then verse two, in Pickthall's words: "We have not revealed unto thee (Muhammad) this Qur'an that thou shouldst be distressed". The word is tashqa: to be wretched, worn out, miserable. It shares a root with the word Zakariyya used in Surah Maryam: I have never been left wretched in my prayer to You. Two surahs in a row, the same root: a man never left wretched by prayer, and a Qur'an not sent to make anyone wretched. Commentators give reasons for the verse. One report says the Prophet stood in night prayer so long his feet swelled. Another says his opponents mocked him: this Qur'an has made you miserable. The verse answers both. Verse three says what the Qur'an is for: a reminder, for whoever stands in awe. A hadith in Bukhari puts it plainly: the religion is ease, and nobody makes it hard on themselves except that it overcomes them. So aim for what's right, come close to it, and be of good cheer. This doesn't mean faith asks nothing. Ta-Ha goes on to tell Musa's long story, which is anything but easy. But it begins by saying what the weight is for. Not misery. Reminder.
screen: `TA. HA. THE MEANING IS DEBATED.` · `TASHQA: WORN OUT, WRETCHED.` · `FEET SWOLLEN IN NIGHT PRAYER.` · `THE RELIGION IS EASE.` · then, large: `NOT TO DISTRESS YOU.`

segments.voice: Notice if there's anything you carry about your faith, or about trying to be a good person, that feels like a stone: a guilt, a standard you never meet, a practice you dread. Name it, and ask what it was meant to be for: remembering, rest, connection. If you pray, you can ask for ease in it; if not, just let the stone sit down beside you for a while.
Ta-Ha. The surah that opens by promising the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out, but as a reminder. Today's word.
Your line: the stones were never the point. The weight is for remembering. Day four hundred seventy-five.

476.title: Umar hears Ta-Ha
476.hook: on his way to harm the Prophet ﷺ, Umar reads Ta-Ha at his sister's house and is changed
476.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Umar's conversion from the sirah literature as an example of the Qur'an's power to move a hostile heart; many also honor his sister Fatima's courage in the account.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the opening of Ta-Ha. Your line was the stones were never the point. Today ends a week.

Mecca, some years after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ began to preach. A tall, hot-tempered man named Umar ibn al-Khattab walks fast through the streets with a sword. He's decided the new religion has divided his city long enough, and he's going to end it by killing the man who brought it. On the way, someone stops him: before you fix other people's families, look at your own. Your sister has become a Muslim.

This story comes from Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet, not the Qur'an or Bukhari or Muslim, and the sources tell it with variations, but it's one of the best-loved conversion stories in Muslim memory. Umar goes to his sister Fatima's house. Inside, she and her husband Sa'id are being taught by a companion named Khabbab, reading from a page. They hear Umar coming and hide the page. He bursts in: what was that murmuring I heard? He grabs his brother-in-law, and when his sister steps between them, he strikes her and she bleeds. And she says to his face: yes, we're Muslims. Do what you like. Seeing her blood, Umar is ashamed. He asks for the page. She says: you're not clean; wash first. He washes. And he reads the opening of Ta-Ha: We did not send down the Qur'an to distress you, but as a reminder. When he finished, the report says, he said: how beautiful, how noble these words are. Khabbab comes out of hiding. Umar asks where the Prophet is, goes to the house where the Muslims were meeting, and declares his faith. The man who set out to end the religion became one of its pillars, and later the second caliph. What changed him? Not an argument, not a miracle, not a threat. His sister's courage, and a page of words read slowly. This week ran from Dhul-Qarnayn's wall through Zakariyya's secret call, Yahya's gentleness, Ibrahim's peace, love appointed and Ta-Ha's promise, and it ends on a page in a sister's hands.

chat.says: What made the man who set out to end Islam become a Muslim?

A long debate with the Prophet, who won him over with arguments.
A miracle he saw on the road, which made him drop his sword.
